# A failure of Imagination: VLMs fail to use visual representations for text, but self-distillation can help

Shashwat Singh    He He    Tal Linzen Affiliation: New York University
Email: [{ss20428,hhe,linzen}@nyu.edu](mailto:)

###### Abstract

Vision-language (VL) models are typically built by fine-tuning a
language model to attend to visual features in service of a Visual
Question-Answering objective. We ask whether this alignment changes how
language models represent text—especially on tasks where visualization
would help, like geometry questions posed in words. We distinguish weak
multimodality (the model can answer questions about an input image) from
strong multimodality (the model’s text representations themselves become
vision-aligned, improving performance on text-only tasks with latent
visual structure). To test for strong multimodality, we construct a task
of shape-counting problems with paired equivalent text and image
specifications. This task is trivial when the image is provided, but
requires visualization when specified in text as line coordinates. We
compare instruction-tuned Qwen-2.5 and Mistral models against their
vision-aligned counterparts on the text variant of the task. We find
that the multimodal models do no better in this setting, despite strong
performance on the image version of the task. Probing experiments
corroborate this: vision-aligned decoder embeddings carry no more visual
structure than their text-only counterparts. Finally, we provide an
optimization objective that distills in-context visual embeddings into
text embeddings. This alignment induces gains on the text variant of the
task without explicit task supervision, even on samples more complex
than seen during alignment. This suggests that VQA-style alignment
leaves available cross-modal transfer untapped.

|     |
| --- |
|     |

## 1 Introduction

We study the paradigm of vision language alignment used in the Qwen
([Bai et al., 2025b](#bib.bib13); [Bai et al., 2025a](#bib.bib17)),
LlaVA ([Liu et al., 2023](#bib.bib18)), and Pixtral ([Agrawal et al.,
2024](#bib.bib22)). These models begin with a strong language decoder
that is then aligned with a pretrained vision encoder on a visual
question answering task. Since the visual task feedback is used to
update the language backbone, we ask whether it teaches the language
decoder to build meaningful visual representations of text when useful.

We distinguish between weak multimodality and strong multimodality. A
weakly multimodal model can operate on input from a different modality
(vision) and can answer questions about that input. However, when it
comes to input that is purely in text, a weakly multimodal model will
behave exactly like the language-only model. By contrast, a strongly
multimodal model can form representations for inputs provided in text
that are vision-aligned and consequently perform better when the tasks
are more naturally represented visually (for example, front-end code and
edits, or solving geometry problems specified in words). Informally,
strongly multimodal models treat all modalities as part of the same
cognitive system rather than as separate input pipelines that share a
decoder. We call this capability of a strongly multimodal model
“visualization” in this work. We argue that strong multimodality is
desirable because it would utilize data from a modality (say vision) to
improve performance on another modality (text).

To study visualization in a tractable way, we propose a synthetic task
that has the following properties (i) For each instance, there is a way
to equivalently specify the question in text or image; and (ii) The
problem is much easier when specified visually. Our task consists of
code that draws shapes and the language model is asked questions about
the resulting image (see
section [3](#S3 "3 The Shape Counting Task ‣ A failure of Imagination: VLMs fail to use visual representations for text, but self-distillation can help")).
We evaluate Qwen 2.5 models ([Bai et al., 2025b](#bib.bib13)) and
Pixtral / Mistral Nemo 12B ([Agrawal et al., 2024](#bib.bib22); [Mistral
AI, 2024](#bib.bib23)), which provide a clean minimal pair. We isolate
the contribution of vision-language training to text-only reasoning by
comparing vanilla text decoders to the corresponding VL-aligned text
decoders. For both the model families, we find that vision alignment
provides essentially no benefit on the text task, despite the image
version being significantly easier for the same models. Linear and
Contrastive probes on the decoder’s hidden states confirm that the
visual structure in both models’ decoder representations are equally
bad.

Finally, we address whether visualization – beyond what text training
alone provides– can be instilled at all. We propose an alignment method
based on self-distillation: the model is trained to predict, from text,
the embeddings it would have obtained given the image. Applied to our
synthetic data (where paired samples are available) with no explicit
task supervision, this yields substantial improvements on the text
version of the task across difficulty levels. This provides a proof of
concept that alignment objectives aimed at strong multimodality, by
targeting text representations directly, can yield gains on this task
that VQA-style alignment does not.

##### Contributions.

Our contributions are three-fold:

- •
  A new task that can be equivalently specified visually and in text,
  but is much easier to solve using visual representations. This allows
  us to evaluate the same models on the vision-specified version of the
  task and the text-specified version of the task while controlling for
  difficulty. Additionally, it also allows us to compare vision-aligned
  text decoders to pure text decoders with the upper-bound context of
  vision informed performance.
- •
  We present behavioral and representational evidence that for two
  widely used VL model families (Qwen 2.5 VL, Pixtral), the
  vision-aligned decoder does not construct visual representations for
  tasks provided in text, even when such representations are useful.
- •
  To demonstrate that stronger multimodality can be instilled in
  multimodal models through better alignment methods, we provide a self
  distillation based method to vision-align a text student to learn to
  use visual representations for textual tasks. With this method, we
  provide a proof-of-concept model that operates on the text version of
  our task but with vision-informed representations – demonstrating
  improvements across the difficulties of the task.

## 2 Related Work

### 2.1 Non-text Representations in Pure Language Models

[Sharma et al. (2024)](#bib.bib8), [Patel and Pavlick
(2022)](#bib.bib10), [Abdou et al. (2021)](#bib.bib11), and [Ilharco et
al. (2021)](#bib.bib9) explore the question of whether visual grounding
(similar to our notion of strong multimodality) emerges in vanilla
language models. [Sharma et al. (2024)](#bib.bib8) operationalize this
in a code generation setting – where they make the language models
generate images from descriptions via code. [Ilharco et al.
(2021)](#bib.bib9) and [Abdou et al. (2021)](#bib.bib11) study whether
language models learn visual relationships from their text training
corpus – [Ilharco et al. (2021)](#bib.bib9) train mappings from BERT
representations of concrete words to representations from a vision model
(Faster R-CNN) and find nontrivial structural alignment while [Abdou et
al. (2021)](#bib.bib11) do this by comparing embeddings to the CIELAB
colour space. Finally, [Patel and Pavlick (2022)](#bib.bib10) study
grounded representations in language models (GPT-2 and GPT-3). Our work
asks a complementary question: what does vision-language alignment
provide beyond language-only training. [Lepori et al.
(2026)](#bib.bib20) show that language models presented with a random
walk over a latent state-space topology come to encode that topology in
their hidden states (replicating [Park et al. (2025)](#bib.bib21)), yet
largely fail to use those representations.

### 2.2 Visual Reasoning

[Xu et al. (2026)](#bib.bib1) and [Wang et al. (2025)](#bib.bib2) both
study vision-language models on geometry tasks. [Xu et al.
(2026)](#bib.bib1) investigate math problems that they can equivalently
transcribe in images, text, and both together. They observe that the
tested models (Qwen-3 ([Bai et al., 2025a](#bib.bib17))) simply do best
on the text-only variants of the problems. [Wang et al.
(2025)](#bib.bib2) likewise report that the contribution of visual
information diminishes on harder problems. These papers study whether
visual information in-context can be effectively leveraged by
vision-language models. By contrast, we study visual representations in
purely textual input. Our setup shares motivation with
MentisOculi ([Zeller et al., 2026](#bib.bib3)), which designs tasks that
require visual reasoning. They demonstrate that visual reasoning in
models that can interleave text and image generation is limited by error
accumulation. Our work differs in task specification: nearly all of
their tasks include an image in the input, and on the one exception
(RushHour) the models they test do worse with visual context than
without. Therefore, this setting does not allow us to answer our more
specific question: In tasks where appropriate, does the vision-aligned
text decoder perform better than a comparable text decoder with no
vision training?. Finally, [Xu et al. (2025)](#bib.bib5) criticize
existing vision-language benchmarks on the grounds that they can be
solved from the text descriptions alone.

### 2.3 Methods: Self-Distillation to Imagine Missing Modalities

[Yang et al. (2025)](#bib.bib4) provide a latent continuous reasoning
methodology. For tasks where one can generate intermediate helper images
for reasoning as training data, they propose training a multimodal model
to generate the image encoding of the intermediate helper images
instead. This is followed by finetuning on the task. Additionally, the
idea of imitating a missing modality has been explored by [Li et al.
(2024)](#bib.bib6) and [Zheng et al. (2022)](#bib.bib7).

## 3 The Shape Counting Task

![Refer to caption](2610.25470v1/plots/code-demo-images/carbon-4.png)

(a) An example code snippet that would draw a configuration of a
rectangle and a trapezium.

![Refer to caption](2610.25470v1/plots/code-demo-images/demo.png)

(b) Output image with one trapezium and one rectangle.

Figure 1: A simple example of the paired data sample: the code snippet
(left) when compiled generates the image (right). The task is simply to
count shapes of each kind given either the code snippet (for the
text-variant of the task) or the rendered image (for the image variant).

We are concerned with problems that can be completely specified in text
but would benefit a lot from intermediate computations in a visual
representation space. To that end, we use a synthetic data setting for
the experiments in this work. We describe it here briefly and provide
the full data generation process in
Appendix [A.1](#A1.SS1 "A.1 Data Generation Protocol ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ A failure of Imagination: VLMs fail to use visual representations for text, but self-distillation can help").
We procedurally generate python code that when run would output a set of
shapes (specifically, rectangles and trapeziums). This allows us to
generate samples of varying difficulties that deterministically specify
an image but do so entirely in text; for an illustrative example, see
Figure [1](#S3.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 3 The Shape Counting Task ‣ A failure of Imagination: VLMs fail to use visual representations for text, but self-distillation can help").
To generate an item, we sample the number of rectangles and trapeziums
in the scene, rotate them randomly, and sample their positions in the
image. We derive from the shapes a list of edges with exact coordinates
that can be turned into a python program (see
Figure [1(a)](#S3.F1.sf1 "In Figure 1 ‣ 3 The Shape Counting Task ‣ A failure of Imagination: VLMs fail to use visual representations for text, but self-distillation can help")).
Crucially, we shuffle the order in which edges appear in the program.
This leaves the rendered image unchanged but forces the model to compose
edges that may be separated by long stretches of code.

## 4 Vision-Language Models Use Poor Visual Representations

##### Scope and Models.

This study examines a popular vision-language alignment paradigm, in
which a pretrained language model is coupled to a vision encoder through
a translation MLP block and trained under some alignment objective
(usually visual question answering). To isolate the effect of alignment
on the language model’s representations, we require minimal pairs of
models, that is, the text decoder before visual adaptation and the
updated weights after visual adaptation. These requirements leave us
with the Qwen-VL family ([Bai et al., 2025b](#bib.bib13); [Bai et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib17)), Mistral / Pixtral ([Mistral AI, 2024](#bib.bib23);
[Agrawal et al., 2024](#bib.bib22)) and LLaVA ([Liu et al.,
2023](#bib.bib18)). Furthermore, we need the VLM to do better on the
image variant of the task than the text variant to conduct the study.
This would validate that our synthetic data is in-distribution and the
vision encoder has the features required for the image variant of the
task. LLaVA fails this criterion but we present its results in
Section [4.1](#S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1 "Results. ‣ 4.1 Behavioral Experiments ‣ 4 Vision-Language Models Use Poor Visual Representations ‣ A failure of Imagination: VLMs fail to use visual representations for text, but self-distillation can help")
for completeness. The analysis in this work centres around Qwen 2.5 and
Pixtral models.

### 4.1 Behavioral Experiments

The task is to count the number of shapes of each type given the source
code. This requires the model to group edges into shapes and identify
the angles in it. However, when the rendered image is available, the
distinction (between rectangles and trapeziums) is obvious using
heuristics in the image. We measure the performance of the model(s) on
the task based on just the image; this establishes our upper-bound
baseline. We then compare text-only models to vision-aligned text models
on different answer modes (No-CoT, ICL-No-CoT, and ICL-CoT). In the
No-CoT condition, the model is provided just with the description of the
task, and is asked to output the answer immediately. In the ICL-No-CoT
condition, the model is provided with the task description as well as
examples of the task (i.e. in-context learning, or ICL), and is asked to
output the answer immediately, Finally, in the ICL-CoT condition, the
model is provided with examples and is allowed to output whatever it
wants before providing the answer. For the image variant of the task,
the model is simply asked to look at the image and count the number of
shapes of each type (for the full prompts, see
Appendix [A.2](#A1.SS2 "A.2 Different Prompts Used ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ A failure of Imagination: VLMs fail to use visual representations for text, but self-distillation can help")).
For all ICL setups, we use $`3`$ ICL examples. We calculate the accuracy
of the task strictly: the model is given a point only if it gets the
count of both the shapes right.

![Refer to caption](2610.25470v1/plots/expt1/experiment_1_12B_72B.png)

Figure 2: When the problem is provided in text, for all the settings
tested—with and without in-context examples (ICL), and with and without
chain of thought (CoT)—the performance of the multimodal models is
similar to their text-only counterparts, and far below the image
ceiling. This indicates that vision alignment did not transfer
visualization capabilities to the text decoder. Error bars are based on
the 95% confidence interval on accuracy estimates using the normal
approximation to the binomial distribution.

##### Results.

The results are shown in
Figure [2](#S4.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 4.1 Behavioral Experiments ‣ 4 Vision-Language Models Use Poor Visual Representations ‣ A failure of Imagination: VLMs fail to use visual representations for text, but self-distillation can help").
When the task is provided visually, the models’ performance sets a high
ceiling. Neither of the text decoders come close to this ceiling on the
text variant of the task. Most importantly, the vision-aligned decoder
performs similarly to the text decoder. While ICL or COT don’t seem to
help our task, they improve the model’s ability to simply count the
total number of shapes (without identifying them). The models can often
group vertices by looking at closed-loops during CoT (see
Appendix [A.7](#A1.SS7 "A.7 How often do models get the total number of shapes right? ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ A failure of Imagination: VLMs fail to use visual representations for text, but self-distillation can help")).
Therefore, we restrict to rectangles and trapeziums as they have the
same number of vertices and distinguishing them requires some estimation
of the angle. Additionally, we ran these experiments on LLaVA and the
corresponding text backbone Llama-Vicuna ([Zheng et al.,
2023](#bib.bib19)). The vision-informed version of the task had an
accuracy of 0.06 and the text variant performances were 0.07 for the
multimodal decoder and 0.09 for the vanilla decoder. As the
vision-informed performance is slightly worse, we exclude LLaVA from the
remaining study.

### 4.2 Limited Evidence for Visual Representations in the Models’ Embeddings

The results in the shape-counting task suggest that vision-language
aligned language decoders are not significantly better than their
language-only counterparts. We next test if the internal representations
of the vision-aligned models have more visual structure than those of
the text-only models. We use both linear probes and contrastive
alignment probes (for details, see
Appendix [A.4.1](#A1.SS4.SSS1 "A.4.1 Linear-Probe Layer Sweep Details ‣ A.4 Experiment Hyper-parameters ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ A failure of Imagination: VLMs fail to use visual representations for text, but self-distillation can help")
and
Appendix [A.4.2](#A1.SS4.SSS2 "A.4.2 Contrastive Text–Image Probe Details ‣ A.4 Experiment Hyper-parameters ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ A failure of Imagination: VLMs fail to use visual representations for text, but self-distillation can help")).

##### Linear Probes

The probe is trained to predict the number of times a particular type of
shape (rectangle or trapezium) appears in the sample. This is a 9-class
classification problem (an image can have $`0-8`$ rectangles). For each
layer, we train separate probes on the mean-pooled representations for
rectangle count and trapezium count.

##### Contrastive Probes

Our dataset consists of paired image-text instances $`(x_{i},y_{i})`$
where $`x_{i}`$ is a rendered image and $`y_{i}`$ is the code that
produces it. We measure the alignment between the text model’s
embeddings of the code and the embeddings of the corresponding image
produced by DiNOv2 ([Oquab et al., 2023](#bib.bib12)), a pure vision
encoder. We also conduct this experiment against a SigLip ([Zhai et al.,
2023](#bib.bib26)) vision encoder. We fit linear projections to the
InfoNCE  ([Oord et al., 2018](#bib.bib15)) (contrastive) loss
popularized by CLIP ([Radford et al., 2021](#bib.bib16)). We refer to
these as _contrastive probes_. We extract a single vector for each: the
CLS token from DINOv2 for $`x_{i}`$, and the mean-pooled hidden state at
layer $`\ell`$ of the text model for $`y_{i}`$. Two linear projections
$`f_{\theta}:\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{img}}}\to\mathbb{R}^{1536}`$ and
$`f_{\phi}:\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{txt}}}\to\mathbb{R}^{1536}`$ map these
into a shared space, where they are L2-normalized. The dimensionality of
the shared space is that of DinoV2-Giant:

|     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
\tilde{z}_{i}^{\text{img}}=\tfrac{f_{\theta}(x_{i})}{\lVert f_{\theta}(x_{i})\rVert_{2}},\qquad\tilde{z}_{i}^{\text{txt}}=\tfrac{f_{\phi}(y_{i})}{\lVert f_{\phi}(y_{i})\rVert_{2}}.
``` |  |

Given a batch of $`N`$ such pairs sampled uniformly from the dataset, we
optimize the symmetric InfoNCE objective with temperature $`\tau=0.5`$:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{L}=-\frac{1}{2N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\left[\log\frac{\exp(\tilde{z}_{i}^{\text{img}}\cdot\tilde{z}_{i}^{\text{txt}}/\tau)}{\sum_{j=1}^{N}\exp(\tilde{z}_{i}^{\text{img}}\cdot\tilde{z}_{j}^{\text{txt}}/\tau)}+\log\frac{\exp(\tilde{z}_{i}^{\text{img}}\cdot\tilde{z}_{i}^{\text{txt}}/\tau)}{\sum_{j=1}^{N}\exp(\tilde{z}_{j}^{\text{img}}\cdot\tilde{z}_{i}^{\text{txt}}/\tau)}\right].
``` |  | (1) |

We report bidirectional top-1 batch retrieval accuracy: instance $`i`$
is correct in the image $`\to`$ text direction if
$`\arg\max_{j}\tilde{z}_{i}^{\text{img}}\cdot\tilde{z}_{j}^{\text{txt}}=i`$,
and analogously for text. We report the average of the two. Because both
projections are linear, the retrieval accuracy can be treated as a proxy
for the similarity in embedding structure between the two sets which we
interpret as degree of visualization behavior. We argue that if the text
model is doing computations that “look like” visualization at some layer
then the representations at that level should have structure similar to
the corresponding image embeddings from a good image encoder. We choose
DiNo-v2 ([Oquab et al., 2023](#bib.bib12)) for the image embeddings as
it is a pure image encoder that was never aligned or supervised by text.
We want to compare the degree of "visualization" between vision-aligned
text models (Qwen-2.5VL, Pixtral) and their non-vision-aligned
counterparts (Qwen-2.5, Mistral-Nemo). On our dataset, we know there is
perfect correspondence between the text and the image data therefore
text embeddings with visual structure should be easier to align with
corresponding image embeddings. See
Figure [4](#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ Probe Controls ‣ 4.2 Limited Evidence for Visual Representations in the Models’ Embeddings ‣ 4 Vision-Language Models Use Poor Visual Representations ‣ A failure of Imagination: VLMs fail to use visual representations for text, but self-distillation can help")
for results and
Appendix [A.4.2](#A1.SS4.SSS2 "A.4.2 Contrastive Text–Image Probe Details ‣ A.4 Experiment Hyper-parameters ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ A failure of Imagination: VLMs fail to use visual representations for text, but self-distillation can help")
for experimental details. To support these results we do the experiment
with SigLip as the image encoder and see consistent results (see
Appendix [A.5](#A1.SS5 "A.5 Contrastive Probes With a SigLip as an Image Encoder ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ A failure of Imagination: VLMs fail to use visual representations for text, but self-distillation can help")).
Additionally, we also conduct this experiment on the COCO dataset ([Lin
et al., 2015](#bib.bib31)), a dataset with real images and free-form
descriptive captions. The semantic correspondence of image-text pairs is
noisier in COCO but the image data is more in-distribution for the image
encoders used.

##### Probe Controls

To rule out easy-to-exploit shortcuts in both probing setups we do a
random model control. For the controls, all the probes are retrained on
top of embeddings calculated by a randomly-initialized language decoder.
Low performance on these control probes implies that the probes measure
properties of the pretrained checkpoints beyond what can be inferred
simply from surface-level statistics in the embeddings.

![Refer to
caption](2610.25470v1/plots/expt2/probe_task/probe_combined_prompt_empty.png)

Figure 3: Vision-alignment does not add more visual structure to the
embeddings of the multimodal model, compared to the text-only model.
While probes trained on the embeddings from both classes of models show
above-chance accuracy, the performance for the two classes of models is
very similar.

![Refer to
caption](2610.25470v1/plots/expt2/probe_contrastive/contrastive_accuracy_shapes_vs_coco_row_12B_72B_dinov2-giant_tbs256_poolcls_prompt_empty.png)

Figure 4: The trends on learnt retrieval corroborate that the multimodal
decoder does not have better visual representations of textual inputs
than the text-only model. Both the embedding sets get significantly
above-chance and above-control retrieval accuracy against DiNo
embeddings – at least in the middle layers. However, the VL embeddings
closely track text embeddings.

##### Results.

Both the linear probes
(Figure [3](#S4.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ Probe Controls ‣ 4.2 Limited Evidence for Visual Representations in the Models’ Embeddings ‣ 4 Vision-Language Models Use Poor Visual Representations ‣ A failure of Imagination: VLMs fail to use visual representations for text, but self-distillation can help"))
and the contrastive probes
(Figure [4](#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ Probe Controls ‣ 4.2 Limited Evidence for Visual Representations in the Models’ Embeddings ‣ 4 Vision-Language Models Use Poor Visual Representations ‣ A failure of Imagination: VLMs fail to use visual representations for text, but self-distillation can help"))
show that, when the input is provided in text, the multimodal models
typically do not encode visual structure better than their vanilla text
counterparts. The contrastive probes on COCO show the same trend; this
provides us with further confidence in our interpretation as the data in
COCO more in-distribution for the image encoders – thereby ruling out
the possibility that the results are an artifact of the data
construction. We see that representational quality with respect to
visualization peaks in the middle layers and then falls back towards the
end, a finding consistent with [Skean et al. (2025)](#bib.bib14). We
also note that all the probes significantly outperform the controls.
These findings together with the behavioral findings suggest that, for
these models, the VQA based vision-alignment paradigm does not add
visual structure beyond what text training already provides.

## 5 Teaching the Model to Visualize

The problem, as identified, is that while vision-language models can pay
attention to vision features to perform question-answering tasks
(including the one we propose), they don’t seem to construct internal
representations that capture the visual structure of the problem. To
encourage cross-modality transfer, we propose a methodology based on
self-distillation. The intuition is that we will make the student model
(initialized as a copy of the V+L teacher model) have the same
intermediate embeddings without the image as the teacher calculates with
the image. The Qwen 2.5 VL model treats vision features the same as
token embeddings during language decoding i.e. vision patch embeddings
are concatenated with text context (details about the Qwen architecture
are in
Appendix [A.3](#A1.SS3 "A.3 Summarising the Qwen 2.5 Architecture ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ A failure of Imagination: VLMs fail to use visual representations for text, but self-distillation can help")).
This allows us to get meaningful transfer by literally equating the
embeddings as opposed to some projection or KL-divergence loss which is
typical in distillation literature. We illustrate this in
Figure [5](#S5.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ 5 Teaching the Model to Visualize ‣ A failure of Imagination: VLMs fail to use visual representations for text, but self-distillation can help").

![Refer to caption](2610.25470v1/plots/distillation_demo.png)

Figure 5: Given paired text-image data our alignment method trains the
model to predict from text (code) the embeddings it would’ve had given
the image. During alignment (left) we provide no task context or answer
labels. During evaluation (right) the model performs the shape counting
task.

##### Setup

Let $`\mathcal{D}=\{(x_{i},y_{i})\}_{i=1}^{N}`$ denote a dataset of
paired image–text examples, where $`x_{i}`$ is an image and
$`y_{i}=(y_{i}^{1},\dots,y_{i}^{T_{i}})`$ is a tokenized text sequence
drawn from a vocabulary $`\mathcal{W}`$. We assume access to a
pretrained vision–language model (VLM) $`f_{\theta}`$ comprising a
vision encoder $`\Phi:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R}^{M\times d}`$ that maps
an image to a sequence of $`M`$ visual embeddings, a text embedding
layer $`\mathcal{E}:\mathcal{W}\to\mathbb{R}^{d}`$, and an $`L`$-layer
transformer decoder $`\mathcal{T}`$ operating on sequences in
$`\mathbb{R}^{d}`$, whose $`\ell`$-th layer produces hidden states in
$`\mathbb{R}^{d}`$ for $`\ell\in\{1,\dots,L\}`$.

##### Teacher and Student

We initialize two copies of the pretrained $`f_{\theta}`$. The *teacher*
hereafter referred to as $`f_{\theta_{T}}`$ retains the full
architecture and is kept frozen throughout training. For the *student*,
we discard the vision encoder; the student has to operate on text tokens
only. Its parameters $`\theta_{S}`$ are trainable and initialized from
$`\theta`$.

##### Input Construction

The teacher consumes the image-embeddings followed by the assistant
token while the student consumes the text embeddings followed by the
assistant token. We denote the assistant token as $`\langle a\rangle`$

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
z_{T}^{(i)}\;=\;\Phi_{\theta_{T}}(x_{i})\,\|\,\mathcal{E}_{\theta_{T}}(\langle a\rangle),\quad z_{S}^{(i)}\;=\;\mathcal{E}_{\theta_{S}}(y_{i})\,\|\,\mathcal{E}_{\theta_{S}}(\langle a\rangle)
``` |  | (2) |

Where $`\|`$ denotes sequence concatenation along the token axis and
$`\mathcal{E}`$, the embedding layer, that applies to each token
independently.

##### Distillation objective.

For each example we perform a single forward pass of the teacher and
student decoders on their respective input embedding sequences and
extract the hidden states at the assistant generation position across
all $`L`$ transformer layers:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle h_{T}^{(i,\ell)}\;=\;\mathcal{T}^{(\ell)}_{\theta_{T}}\!\left(z_{T}^{(i)}\right)\!\big[-1\big],\quad h_{S}^{(i,\ell)}\;=\;\mathcal{T}^{(\ell)}_{\theta_{S}}\!\left(z_{S}^{(i)}\right)\!\big[-1\big],`$ |  | (3) |

for $`\ell=1,\dots,L`$, where $`\mathcal{T}^{(\ell)}(\cdot)[p]`$ returns
the $`\ell`$-th layer hidden state at position $`p`$ and we use $`[-1]`$
to indicate the last in the sequence (which refers to the representation
of $`\langle a\rangle`$ token). The student is trained to match the
teacher’s representations at this position via the layerwise
$`\ell_{2}`$ reconstruction loss. Note that for our experiments we try
two variants of the reconstruction loss: vanilla MSE and normalized MSE;
$`\hat{h}`$ in the following equation represents $`h`$ or
$`\frac{h}{\|h\|_{2}}`$, respectively. We find that normalized MSE works
better and report the corresponding results in
Figure [6](#S5.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ 5.1 Experiment ‣ 5 Teaching the Model to Visualize ‣ A failure of Imagination: VLMs fail to use visual representations for text, but self-distillation can help").

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{L}(\theta_{S})\;=\;\mathbb{E}_{(x_{i},y_{i})\sim\mathcal{D}}\left[\,\frac{1}{L\,d}\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\big\lVert\hat{h}_{S}^{(i,\ell)}\,-\,\operatorname{sg}\!\big(\hat{h}_{T}^{(i,\ell)}\big)\big\rVert_{2}^{2}\,\right],
``` |  | (4) |

where $`\operatorname{sg}(\cdot)`$ denotes the stop-gradient operator,
reflecting that the teacher is frozen. Note that the teacher conditions
on $`x_{i}`$ via $`\Phi(x_{i})`$ while the student conditions on
$`y_{i}`$; the loss therefore forces $`\theta_{S}`$ to encode, from
$`y_{i}`$, the internal state the multimodal teacher would have formed
from $`x_{i}`$.

### 5.1 Experiment

![Refer to caption](2610.25470v1/plots/expt_3/best_combined_maxval.png)

Figure 6: In all settings the distilled model outperforms the base
models on across-shape accuracy even beyond the alignment cutoff, that
is, the maximum number of shapes the distilled model has seen in a
single sample. All the subplots represent the same set of samples – just
with different prompts. All the models in this experiment are 7B models
(Qwen 2.5 Instruct and Qwen 2.5 VL Instruct).

##### Alignment and Length Generalization

We experiment with a Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct model; we use a 7B model, as
opposed to the 72B or 12B models used earlier, because of compute
constraints. Crucially, during alignment, neither the student nor the
teacher is provided with a specification of the task (an instruction to
count the number of shapes) or task labels (the counts). Therefore, any
transfer comes from the teacher’s task-agnostic processing of the image.
These image-conditioned representations are informative about properties
such as shape counts, even though the teacher is never prompted to
attend to them; this is precisely the kind of general visual structure
we aim to transfer. To test for generalization, we only align the model
on samples corresponding to a maximum of $`4`$ shapes per image (and
code). Then, as in
section [4.1](#S4.SS1 "4.1 Behavioral Experiments ‣ 4 Vision-Language Models Use Poor Visual Representations ‣ A failure of Imagination: VLMs fail to use visual representations for text, but self-distillation can help"),
we evaluate on a completely held-out set all the way up till $`8`$
shapes, this time with prompts and task specification. The experiment
demonstrates: 1. Task agnostic alignment 2. Length generalization of
alignment. The results are shown in
Figure [6](#S5.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ 5.1 Experiment ‣ 5 Teaching the Model to Visualize ‣ A failure of Imagination: VLMs fail to use visual representations for text, but self-distillation can help").
Note that all of them represent performance on the same set of samples
and only the instruction prompts are different for the text inputs. The
image performance curve is on the same instructions prompt for all the
subplots. We provide the different instructions used in
Appendix [A.2](#A1.SS2 "A.2 Different Prompts Used ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ A failure of Imagination: VLMs fail to use visual representations for text, but self-distillation can help").
See
Appendix [A.4.3](#A1.SS4.SSS3 "A.4.3 Distillation Training Details ‣ A.4 Experiment Hyper-parameters ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ A failure of Imagination: VLMs fail to use visual representations for text, but self-distillation can help")
for other details.

##### Results

Figure [6](#S5.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ 5.1 Experiment ‣ 5 Teaching the Model to Visualize ‣ A failure of Imagination: VLMs fail to use visual representations for text, but self-distillation can help")
shows that just the objective of predicting image-informed embeddings
from the same model can show very strong gains on the text version of
the task. The distillation model usually outperforms the vanilla text
decoder and the multimodal decoder. It is important to note that the
task was not specified during alignment – this suggests that image
encoder does process the images in a generic way that is useful for the
task post-facto and hence learning to imitate that computation allows
our language model to visualize. The performance gains continue beyond
the alignment cutoff, suggesting the stronger visual representations
imparted by our distillation method generalize to samples that are
harder to process than the ones used for alignment. We note that the
gains in the ICL settings are modest, but this experiment is only
intended as a proof-of-concept.

##### Language Evaluations

We evaluate our distilled artifact on unrelated language benchmarks to
check whether the distillation has catastrophic effects on language
modeling. The distilled models show little to no degradation, See
Appendix [A.6](#A1.SS6 "A.6 LM Evaluations ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ A failure of Imagination: VLMs fail to use visual representations for text, but self-distillation can help").

## 6 Discussion

We test minimal pairs of language-only and vision-and-language models,
on a task that can be equivalently specified in both text and image, but
where the image version is substantially easier. We demonstrate that the
standard vision-language alignment paradigm like in Qwen 2.5-VL and
Pixtral do not make the language modeling backbone meaningfully better
at text tasks that benefit from visualization. We conduct this analysis
at two levels: behavioral and representational. Behaviorally, the
vision-aligned text decoder and the vanilla text decoder perform
comparably poorly on the text variant of our shape-counting task,
lagging significantly behind the performance of the multimodal model
when it is given the rendered image. Our representational probes show
some evidence of visual structure emerging in the middle layers of both
classes of models, but, crucially, the vision-aligned decoders’
embeddings are typically on par with or worse than those of the vanilla
text models. Together, these findings suggest that for models we study
the VQA-based vision-alignment paradigm does not transfer vision priors
into the language decoder’s text-processing pathway: it only teaches the
model to attend to visual features when they are present, and not to
think visually about text.

A natural objection to this conclusion is that text training alone may
already saturate whatever visual structure a language model can
plausibly acquire. Prior work on emergent grounding in pure language
models ([Abdou et al., 2021](#bib.bib11); [Sharma et al.,
2024](#bib.bib8); [Patel and Pavlick, 2022](#bib.bib10)) has shown that
nontrivial perceptual structure emerges in model that have only been
trained on text. We address this objection with our distillation
experiment. By aligning the Qwen-2.5-VL-7B text decoder so that, given a
textual input, it reconstructs the hidden states the same model would
produce given the corresponding image—without any task supervision—we
induce measurable improvements on the text variant of our task. These
gains length-generalize beyond the shape counts seen during alignment
training. We interpret these results as a proof of concept for vision
alignment that bleeds into the text pathways of a language model
allowing it to use vision-informed representations for text tasks that
benefit.

We view our work as a call to review how vision-language alignment
training is usually done i.e. visual alignment of a language model is
mostly seen as a way for it to process images. Our results suggest that
this does not, by itself, provide strong multimodality. If our goal is
to get strong multimodality then alignment strategies that make the
language model better at text tasks like the self distillation we
demonstrate deserve more attention

## 7 Limitations

The results demonstrated in this work including the proposed alignment
methodology has been conducted on a single synthetic setup. Future work
should expand the scope to other evaluative setups where the image-based
performance is significantly better than the equivalently specified
text-based performance cleanly. Furthermore, the distillation results
are provided as a proof of concept. We leave adapting to scale of data
for production-ready models to future work.

## Appendix A Appendix

### A.1 Data Generation Protocol

Each sample consists of a small scene of non-overlapping shapes placed
along a random walk on a 2D plane, together with a shuffled list of the
edge lengths of those shapes. The generation procedure is summarized in
Algorithm [1](#alg1 "Algorithm 1 ‣ Output. ‣ A.1 Data Generation Protocol ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ A failure of Imagination: VLMs fail to use visual representations for text, but self-distillation can help");
we describe its components here.

##### Shapes and directions.

We draw shapes from the set
$`\mathcal{S}=\{\texttt{rectangle},\texttt{trapezium}\}`$. A rectangle
is parameterized by two side lengths $`(a,b)`$, and an isosceles
trapezium by its top length $`t`$, bottom length $`b`$, and height
$`h`$. For each shape we deterministically construct its vertices at the
origin via the helpers RectVertices and TrapVertices, and connect them
into a closed polygon with CyclicEdges.

Placements are connected by unit steps in one of four cardinal
directions,
$`\mathcal{D}=\{\texttt{up},\texttt{down},\texttt{left},\texttt{right}\}`$,
with associated unit vectors $`\{\mathbf{e}_{d}\}_{d\in\mathcal{D}}`$.
Successive shapes are placed at positions $`p_{1},p_{2},\ldots`$ where
$`p_{i+1}=p_{i}+\rho\,\mathbf{e}_{c_{i}}`$ and $`\rho>0`$ controls the
spacing.

##### Sampling procedure.

Given a sample, we first draw the number of shapes
$`n\sim\mathrm{Uniform}\{1,\ldots,N_{\max}\}`$, their types
$`s_{1},\ldots,s_{n}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{i.i.d.}}}{{\sim}}\mathrm{Uniform}(\mathcal{S})`$,
and the step directions
$`c_{1},\ldots,c_{n-1}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{i.i.d.}}}{{\sim}}\mathrm{Uniform}(\mathcal{D})`$
between successive placements. For each shape $`i`$ we draw its
dimensions uniformly from $`[\ell_{\min},\ell_{\max}]`$ (and
additionally $`h_{i}\in[h_{\min},h_{\max}]`$ for trapezia), construct
its vertices at the origin, and apply a rotation by
$`\theta_{i}\sim\mathrm{Uniform}(\Theta)`$ followed by a translation to
$`p_{i}`$. Letting $`R(\theta)`$ denote the $`2\times 2`$ rotation
matrix, each edge $`(u,v)`$ of shape $`i`$ contributes the rotated,
translated edge
$`\big(R(\theta_{i})u+p_{i},\,R(\theta_{i})v+p_{i}\big)`$ to the global
edge set $`E`$.

##### Output.

Given the final edge set $`E`$, we sample a random permutation
$`\sigma`$ of its elements and return the sequence of edge lengths
$`\mathcal{P}=(\ell(e_{\sigma(1)}),\ldots,\ell(e_{\sigma(|E|)}))`$
together with a rendered image of the scene. The shuffling forces the
text version to require the model to compose edges separated by other
lines of code.

1: $`N_{\max}`$, $`[\ell_{\min},\ell_{\max}]`$, $`[h_{\min},h_{\max}]`$,
$`\rho`$, $`\Theta`$

2: $`n\sim\mathrm{Uniform}\{1,\ldots,N_{\max}\}`$

3:
$`s_{i}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{i.i.d.}}}{{\sim}}\mathrm{Uniform}(\mathcal{S})`$
for $`i=1,\ldots,n`$

4:
$`c_{i}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{i.i.d.}}}{{\sim}}\mathrm{Uniform}(\mathcal{D})`$
for $`i=1,\ldots,n-1`$

5: $`p_{1}\leftarrow\mathbf{0}`$; $`E\leftarrow\emptyset`$

6: for $`i=1,\ldots,n`$ do

7:   $`\theta_{i}\sim\mathrm{Uniform}(\Theta)`$

8:   if $`s_{i}=\texttt{rectangle}`$ then

9:
   $`(a_{i},b_{i})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{i.i.d.}}}{{\sim}}\mathrm{Uniform}([\ell_{\min},\ell_{\max}])^{2}`$

10:    $`V_{i}\leftarrow\textsc{RectVertices}(a_{i},b_{i})`$

11:   else$`\triangleright`$ $`s_{i}=\texttt{trapezium}`$

12:
   $`(t_{i},b_{i})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{i.i.d.}}}{{\sim}}\mathrm{Uniform}([\ell_{\min},\ell_{\max}])^{2}`$

13:    $`h_{i}\sim\mathrm{Uniform}([h_{\min},h_{\max}])`$

14:    $`V_{i}\leftarrow\textsc{TrapVertices}(t_{i},b_{i},h_{i})`$

15:   end if

16:   $`E_{i}\leftarrow\textsc{CyclicEdges}(V_{i})`$

17:
  $`E\leftarrow E\cup\big\{\big(R(\theta_{i})\,u+p_{i},\ R(\theta_{i})\,v+p_{i}\big):(u,v)\in E_{i}\big\}`$

18:   if $`i<n`$ then

19:    $`p_{i+1}\leftarrow p_{i}+\rho\cdot\mathbf{e}_{c_{i}}`$

20:   end if

21: end for

22: $`\sigma\sim\mathrm{Uniform}(\mathrm{Permutations}(E))`$

23:
$`\mathcal{P}\leftarrow\big(e_{\sigma(1)},\ldots,e_{\sigma(|E|)}\big)`$

24: return $`(\mathcal{P},\textsc{Render}(\mathcal{P}))`$

Algorithm 1 Sample generation

### A.3 Summarising the Qwen 2.5 Architecture

We provide a summary description of the Qwen 2.5 VL models here to help
with the intuition behind some design decisions for the distillation
objective specified in
Section [5](#S5 "5 Teaching the Model to Visualize ‣ A failure of Imagination: VLMs fail to use visual representations for text, but self-distillation can help").

The Qwen 2.5 VL models ([Bai et al., 2025b](#bib.bib13)) consist of
three main components (i) the vision encoder which is a ViT with some
efficiency modifications (ii) an MLP-based vision-language merger
component (iii) Large Language Model which starts off as the Qwen 2.5
LM. An inference forward pass goes through the following: the image is
processed by the ViT and the corresponding features are passed through
the MLP merger block, following this the patch vectors are simply put in
the context of the language model like the embedding of any other token.
The Language Model decoder attends to the image information and the text
information auto-regressively.

The vision encoder is pre-trained using a CLIP-style objective first. In
the second-stage, all the components including the vision encoder, the
MLP-merger, and the language model are kept un-frozen and trained for a
visual question answering task. This is followed by a third stage to
adapt the model to work with long-context videos.

### A.4 Experiment Hyper-parameters

#### A.4.1 Linear-Probe Layer Sweep Details

Hyperparameters for the linear probe from
Section [4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2 Limited Evidence for Visual Representations in the Models’ Embeddings ‣ 4 Vision-Language Models Use Poor Visual Representations ‣ A failure of Imagination: VLMs fail to use visual representations for text, but self-distillation can help").

- •
  Layers swept: We conduct the probing experiments on evenly spaced 6
  layers for each of the models.
- •
  Inference: bfloat16 with FlashAttention-2 under HuggingFace tensor
  parallelism (torchrun, one process per GPU, all visible GPUs).
- •
  Pooling: mean-pooling.
- •
  Optimizer: Adam, learning rate $`10^{-3}`$ (PyTorch defaults
  otherwise); no weight decay, no gradient clipping.
- •
  Schedule: at most 100 epochs with early stopping on validation loss
  (patience 10).
- •
  Batch size: 32 (train/val/test); training batches are *not* shuffled.
- •
  Precision / hardware: probe trains in fp32 on a single GPU.
- •
  Data: $`12{,}000`$ synthetic scenes, at most 8 shapes, sizes in
  $`[20,100]`$ px, random rotation, $`10`$ px padding, shuffled
  description lines; sequential (not random) 80/10/10
  train/validation/test split. Text embeddings only — no images are
  used.
- •
  Metrics: macro-averaged accuracy, precision, and recall per head.

#### A.4.2 Contrastive Text–Image Probe Details

Hyperparameters for the contrastive probe from
Section [4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2 Limited Evidence for Visual Representations in the Models’ Embeddings ‣ 4 Vision-Language Models Use Poor Visual Representations ‣ A failure of Imagination: VLMs fail to use visual representations for text, but self-distillation can help").

- •
  Text embeddings: extracted exactly as in
  Appendix [A.4.1](#A1.SS4.SSS1 "A.4.1 Linear-Probe Layer Sweep Details ‣ A.4 Experiment Hyper-parameters ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ A failure of Imagination: VLMs fail to use visual representations for text, but self-distillation can help")
  (same models, same six layers, same random re-initialization,
  masked-mean pooling, bfloat16 tensor-parallel inference).
- •
  Image embeddings: frozen DINOv2-giant, final-layer CLS token
  (dimension $`1536`$); the image-side layer is *not* swept. Images are
  rendered from the same scene descriptions, so each sample yields an
  aligned (text, image) pair. For SigLIP, the image embedding and shared
  projection dimension is 1152.
- •
  Probe: one linear projection per modality; shared projection dimension
  $`=\min(d_{\text{text}},d_{\text{image}})`$), with no hidden layers or
  activations.
- •
  Loss: symmetric InfoNCE on $`\ell_{2}`$-normalized projections —
  cross-entropy over the in-batch similarity matrix, averaged over the
  text$`\to`$image and image$`\to`$text directions — with a fixed
  temperature of $`0.5`$.
- •
  Optimizer: Adam, learning rate $`10^{-3}`$; no early stopping, no
  gradient clipping.
- •
  Schedule: 10 epochs.
- •
  Batch size: 256; batches drawn by a repeated-shuffle sampler with
  sample multiplier 1.5 (each “epoch” covers 1.5 shuffled passes; no
  sample appears twice within a batch). The same sampler is used for
  validation and test, so evaluation metrics average over $`\sim`$1.5
  shuffled passes of the split.
- •
  Precision / hardware: probe trains in fp32 on a single GPU.
- •
  Data: same generation settings and sequential 80/10/10 split as
  Appendix [A.4.1](#A1.SS4.SSS1 "A.4.1 Linear-Probe Layer Sweep Details ‣ A.4 Experiment Hyper-parameters ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ A failure of Imagination: VLMs fail to use visual representations for text, but self-distillation can help")
  ($`12{,}000`$ samples, $`9{,}600`$ train).
- •
  Evaluation: in-batch retrieval accuracy — within each batch of 256
  pairs, the fraction of samples whose highest cosine similarity is
  their true counterpart, averaged over both retrieval directions
  (chance $`=1/256`$).

For the COCO variant of the contrastive probe experiment, everything is
identical except the dataset. We use the train / val / test splits from
the actual dataset.

#### A.4.3 Distillation Training Details

Hyperparameters for the distillation experiment from
Section [5](#S5 "5 Teaching the Model to Visualize ‣ A failure of Imagination: VLMs fail to use visual representations for text, but self-distillation can help").

- •
  Optimizer: AdamW, learning rate $`5\times 10^{-5}`$ (selected from a
  sweep over $`\{10^{-6},5\times 10^{-6},10^{-5},5\times 10^{-5}\}`$);
  PyTorch defaults otherwise ($`\beta=(0.9,0.999)`$,
  $`\epsilon=10^{-8}`$, weight decay $`0.01`$).
- •
  Schedule: cosine decay with linear warmup over the first $`1{,}000`$
  steps, decaying over the estimated total number of training steps;
  stepped per optimizer step.
- •
  Gradient clipping: global norm $`1.0`$ (computed collectively across
  FSDP shards).
- •
  Epochs: We early-stop based on performance on a held-out validation
  set. The reported results are for the 10th epoch of a 40 epoch run.
- •
  Batch size: 4
- •
  Precision: full fp32 (no mixed precision).

The best model across sweeps was picked based on performance on a
held-out validation set of 2000 samples. The test set consists of
$`6{,}000`$ held-out samples.

### A.5 Contrastive Probes With a SigLip as an Image Encoder

We support the results of the contrastive probes in
Section [4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2 Limited Evidence for Visual Representations in the Models’ Embeddings ‣ 4 Vision-Language Models Use Poor Visual Representations ‣ A failure of Imagination: VLMs fail to use visual representations for text, but self-distillation can help")
by rerunning them with a different image encoder as the “image
reference”. Specifically, we use SigLIP ([Zhai et al.,
2023](#bib.bib26)).

![Refer to
caption](2610.25470v1/plots/expt2/probe_contrastive/contrastive_accuracy_shapes_vs_coco_row_12B_72B_siglip-so400m-patch14-384_tbs256_poolcls_prompt_empty.png)

Figure 7: We observe the same trend as in
Figure [4](#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ Probe Controls ‣ 4.2 Limited Evidence for Visual Representations in the Models’ Embeddings ‣ 4 Vision-Language Models Use Poor Visual Representations ‣ A failure of Imagination: VLMs fail to use visual representations for text, but self-distillation can help")
i.e. the text embeddings from the text-only and the VL models show
similar propensity to align with the corresponding image embeddings. The
absolute numbers are higher than seen in
Figure [4](#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ Probe Controls ‣ 4.2 Limited Evidence for Visual Representations in the Models’ Embeddings ‣ 4 Vision-Language Models Use Poor Visual Representations ‣ A failure of Imagination: VLMs fail to use visual representations for text, but self-distillation can help")
because siglip image embeddings are pre-trained with text supervision
and it is not a “pure” image encoder.

### A.6 LM Evaluations

These evaluations were run using the LM-Eval harness ([Gao et al.,
2023](#bib.bib24)). We run the commonsense 0 shot setting, which
consists of evaluating on Multiple-Choice questions on Arc
challenge ([Clark et al., 2018](#bib.bib27)), Hellaswag ([Zellers et
al., 2019](#bib.bib28)), PIQA ([Bisk et al., 2019](#bib.bib29)), and
Winogrande [Sakaguchi et al. (2019)](#bib.bib30). We also run a 5-shot
ICL setting on MMLU ([Hendrycks et al., 2021](#bib.bib25)). See results
in
Table [1](#A1.T1 "Table 1 ‣ A.6 LM Evaluations ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ A failure of Imagination: VLMs fail to use visual representations for text, but self-distillation can help").

|                               | VL     | Text   | Distilled |
|-------------------------------|--------|--------|-----------|
| Commonsense 0 Shot (Accuracy) | 60.33% | 59.39% | 59.10%    |
| MMLU (macro avg)              | 72.49% | 74.66% | 70.14%    |

Table 1: There is minimal to no degradation from the initialized VL
checkpoint due to the distillation.

### A.7 How often do models get the total number of shapes right?

We note that models can get the total number of shapes right without
identifying them by performing a closed-loop analysis as previously
mentioned in
Section [4.1](#S4.SS1 "4.1 Behavioral Experiments ‣ 4 Vision-Language Models Use Poor Visual Representations ‣ A failure of Imagination: VLMs fail to use visual representations for text, but self-distillation can help").
They can look for cycles in the vertices and group them to deduce
shapes. For our largest model (Qwen 2.5 72B), the COT setting really
helps in getting the shape count variant right. See
Figure [8](#A1.F8 "Figure 8 ‣ A.7 How often do models get the total number of shapes right? ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ A failure of Imagination: VLMs fail to use visual representations for text, but self-distillation can help").

![Refer to
caption](2610.25470v1/plots/expt1/experiment_1_12B_72B_count.png)

Figure 8: The models perform much better at the easier sub-task of
getting the total number of shapes in a sample.

### A.8 Probe Results on Distilled Artifacts

We run the probe experiments from
Section [4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2 Limited Evidence for Visual Representations in the Models’ Embeddings ‣ 4 Vision-Language Models Use Poor Visual Representations ‣ A failure of Imagination: VLMs fail to use visual representations for text, but self-distillation can help")
on our distilled artifacts from
Section [5](#S5 "5 Teaching the Model to Visualize ‣ A failure of Imagination: VLMs fail to use visual representations for text, but self-distillation can help").
The distillation objective, in some sense, is a literalisation of our
strong multimodality principle as an optimization objective. Therefore,
if the probes are measuring the right proxy, we should see a strong
difference in trends for the distilled model on those experiments
compared to the release models. We present these results in
Figure [9](#A1.F9 "Figure 9 ‣ A.8 Probe Results on Distilled Artifacts ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ A failure of Imagination: VLMs fail to use visual representations for text, but self-distillation can help")
and
Figure [10](#A1.F10 "Figure 10 ‣ A.8 Probe Results on Distilled Artifacts ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ A failure of Imagination: VLMs fail to use visual representations for text, but self-distillation can help")
and see that the distilled model’s representations not only perform
better on the probing task but also lend themselves better for the
contrastive (retrieval) task against an unrelated image encoder. This is
consistent with the probes tracking the property the distillation
targets, though in-distribution fine-tuning may also raise probe
accuracy.
````
